A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TIS-DPO work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added Appendices F–K.

before.justification: V1 reports original alignment and summarization experiments, ablations, training curves and token-weight case studies in Section 7 and Appendix D.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds experiments on computational budgets, annotation noise, hyperparameters, token-weight consistency, UltraFeedback and positional weight decay.

M1.justification: The main TIS-DPO objective and three contrastive-model construction methods remain unchanged. Appendix K.2 introduces and evaluates an additional procedure multiplying each token's estimated weight by a position-dependent decay factor, lambda^(N−1). This is a limited methodological extension.

E1.justification: Appendix J adds UltraFeedback preference data, described as including general dialogue, reasoning, mathematics and multi-turn conversations. The existing PKU-SafeRLHF, Anthropic-HH, TL;DR and evaluation datasets remain. This broadens data coverage within the retained preference-alignment task and MT-bench evaluation framework.

E2.justification: The comparator memberships in Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 remain unchanged. Added appendix experiments reuse existing comparison methods. Table 7's DPO (reversed) matches the DPO-Negative procedure already described as a comparison in v1 Section 7.4; its new numerical results do not establish a different baseline method.

E3.justification: V2 adds several evaluation designs: three-epoch DPO versus one-epoch TIS-DPO for a stated computational-budget comparison; 20% preference-label swaps; sweeps over weight parameters and clipping bounds; and GPT-4 token-identification evaluation using average weight and rank percentile. Appendix J additionally uses Llama3-8B and reports turn-specific MT-bench scores. These supplement the unchanged original settings.

E4.justification: V1's weight ablations, reward trajectories and qualitative case studies are retained. Appendices F–I and K add computational-budget controls, annotation-noise robustness, hyperparameter sensitivity, quantitative agreement with GPT-4 token selections, positional-weight analysis and a decay intervention. These substantially expand investigation of the method's reliability and mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. V2's added tables continue reporting point estimates. The revised theoretical concentration bound is not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 retain their results, while Tables 3–8 and Figure 8 add substantial new evidence. For example, Table 4 reports 65.2% safety for DPO and 93.2% for TIS-DPO(D) under 20% annotation noise; Table 8 reports 96.7% without positional decay and 97.9% with it. These are newly reported comparisons, not changed scores for the retained main experiments.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix A.2 are substantively revised. V1 uses two Hoeffding bounds combined through a union bound with a chosen deviation parameter. V2 replaces this with a McDiarmid bound explicitly involving the expected winning–losing reward gap and bounded token-reward changes, supported by a new derivation. The remaining principal derivations are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: importance sampling toward an ideal token-reward distribution, three contrastive-model weight estimators, and improved alignment and summarization. Rewritten contribution bullets and the expanded conclusion largely restate these claims rather than redefine their scientific scope.

C2.justification: The added appendices substantially expand interpretation and limitations: computational tradeoffs, annotation-noise resilience, degradation with very wide clipping bounds, unavailable ground-truth token weights, limitations of GPT-4 token selection, applicability to diverse preference data, and positional bias attributed to contrastive DPO training. These go beyond v1's existing discussion of prompt-distribution mismatch and imperfect weight estimation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a new GPT-4 token-identification prompt, parameter-sweep ranges, computational-budget descriptions and the positional-decay coefficient lambda = 0.995. Existing optimizer, hardware and contrastive-training details remain. These are useful additional disclosures, without a comprehensive revision of reproducibility information.

R1.justification: V2 adds the UltraFeedback citation to Cui et al. and removes Hoeffding's reference and two Liu et al. references concerning watermarking and misinformation. Its positioning relative to DPO, TDPO and contrastive alignment remains substantially unchanged. Consolidating the duplicate TDPO preprint and conference references is bibliographic cleanup.

P1.justification: V2 condenses contribution bullets, adds section introductions, expands the conclusion and introduces acknowledgements and conference-header information. The main section order and most retained prose remain stable. The added scientific appendices do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds six appendix tables, the two-panel positional-weight Figure 8 and a boxed token-evaluation prompt. Conference formatting also changes typography, link colors and placement of retained tables and figures. Together these substantially expand and revise the presentation of evidence; Figures 1–7 remain represented.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the noise, sensitivity and token-consistency experiments provide useful additional scrutiny of practical reliability. Reporting issues limit the gains: Appendix F's cost-equivalence argument is not reconciled with Appendix B.2's three-epoch SFT setup, and Figure 8 shows negative mean 'weights' without explaining their relationship to Equation 19's positive weights. The revision improves empirical examination, but these ambiguities prevent a stronger overall quality judgment.
